description: We are a multidisciplinary team of students brought together by a shared interest in space, technology, creativity, and problem-solving. By combining our different skills and perspectives, we aim to create an engaging and innovative solution inspired by real-world space challenges. Through NASA Space Apps, we are excited to learn, collaborate, challenge ourselves, and turn our ideas into something meaningful.

Our project is a 3D space mission simulation game developed using Godot. We have built a working rocket prototype featuring a rocket-building system where players assemble different parts. The game checks part compatibility and informs players if components can work together or need to be changed. It also simulates thrust, fuel consumption, weight, stability, steering, and stage separation, while displaying flight data such as speed, altitude, and fuel levels. After each launch, players receive feedback on success or failure, understand their mistakes, and improve their designs for the next attempt.

Our research uses NASA resources and scientific references to understand real rocket components and space mission requirements.

Future development will expand the game into complete space missions, including scientific equipment for experiments and sample collection, onboard systems for oxygen, power, and life support, and astronaut food supplies. We also aim to introduce space food production concepts, such as beta-carotene production using yeast, inspired by NASA BioNutrients research.

Our goal is to make space mission planning an interactive and practical learning experience.
details:
Our project is a 3D space mission simulation game developed using Godot. It aims to turn the process of planning and executing a space mission into an interactive educational experience. Instead of simply launching a rocket, players learn how different engineering decisions, scientific objectives, and limited resources work together to determine the success of a mission.

How Does the Project Work?

We have developed a working prototype that allows players to build and simulate their own rockets. The rocket is inspired by NASA's Saturn V, which launched the Apollo 11 mission to the Moon.

Players can assemble rockets using separate components, such as fuel tanks, engines, and couplers. Each component has its own properties, including mass, fuel capacity, thrust power, and fuel consumption. Our building system checks component connections and compatibility, warning players when selected parts cannot be properly connected or work together.

After building the rocket, players can launch it and observe its performance through a physics-based simulation. The prototype includes rocket movement, acceleration, steering, stability, fuel consumption, engine thrust control, aerodynamic stabilization using fins, and stage separation using couplers. A camera follows the rocket, while the interface displays real-time flight information, including speed, altitude, fuel level, and the current rocket stage.

After each launch, the game evaluates the result and provides feedback about the attempt. This helps players understand what worked, identify mistakes, and improve their rocket designs in future attempts.

Future Development and Space Mission Planning

Our long-term goal is to expand the prototype into a complete space mission simulator. We plan to introduce a reverse-planning system in which players begin with a scientific objective rather than starting with the rocket itself.

Players will first select the scientific goal of their mission, determine which samples they need to collect or study, and choose the scientific instruments required for observation, experiments, sample collection, and analysis.

They will also prepare the spacecraft's internal systems, including oxygen supply, electrical power, temperature control, and life-support systems. In addition, players will manage astronauts' essential resources, especially water and food. Future features may include ready-made space meals and food-production concepts such as hydroponics and beta-carotene production using yeast, inspired by NASA's BioNutrients research.

The player will then use these mission requirements to determine the necessary spacecraft equipment and design a suitable rocket capable of carrying the required systems, instruments, and resources.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The project makes space engineering more accessible by allowing players to learn through experimentation rather than theory alone. It introduces concepts such as rocket physics, fuel management, mass, thrust, stability, component compatibility, scientific instruments, and mission planning.

It also encourages critical thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and resource management. Players can experiment with different designs, see the consequences of their decisions, learn from unsuccessful attempts, and gradually develop a better understanding of how real space missions are planned.

Our intended impact is to inspire students and beginners to explore space science and engineering while making complex scientific and technical concepts easier to understand through gameplay.

Tools and Technologies

We developed the game using Godot Engine and GDScript. Our development process includes 3D models, physics simulation, rocket components, scripts, user interface elements, camera systems, and particle effects. We also use AI-assisted tools to support parts of the development process and help improve visual assets and the overall presentation of the game.

Our research is guided by NASA's educational resources and scientific references, which help us understand rocket engineering, spacecraft systems, and the requirements of scientific missions.

Creativity and Factors Considered

The creative aspect of our project is the combination of rocket construction, engineering simulation, scientific exploration, and resource management within one interactive experience. The player is not simply controlling a rocket; they are making decisions that affect an entire mission.

Our team considered several important factors, including limited budgets, rocket mass, fuel capacity, thrust, fuel consumption, stability, component compatibility, and the relationship between a mission's scientific objectives and the equipment required to achieve them.

We also considered the importance of spacecraft power, life-support systems, astronaut food and water, and the scientific instruments needed to complete future missions.

We aim to develop an experience that balances educational value, creativity, accessibility, and engineering concepts, while continuously improving the game through testing and iteration.
